summary.text: At \(n=67\), the distinct inputs \(147\) and \(2055\) have residue tuples \((1,3,3,3,19,19,19)\) and \((1,3,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7)\), respectively, each summing to \(67\). Hence the multiplicity at \(67\) is at least two, contradicting the claimed value of one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be sequence A049802, where \(m\bmod 2^k\) denotes the least nonnegative residue of \(m\) modulo \(2^k\). By definition, \(a(n)\), sequence A383327, is the number of indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\). In the finite formulation used here, for \(n>0\) one counts such indices in the range
\[
0\le m<2^{n+1};
\]
this is a sufficient range for all occurrences. For the disproof it is enough merely to exhibit two distinct indices in this range having value \(67\).

We compute \(F(147)\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\), so the relevant moduli are \(2,4,8,16,32,64,128\). Write
\[
147=128+19.
\]
Because \(128\) is divisible by each of these powers of two, the residues of \(147\) equal the corresponding residues of \(19\). They are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
2^k&2&4&8&16&32&64&128\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(19\equiv1\pmod2\), \(19\equiv3\pmod4\), \(19\equiv3\pmod8\), \(19\equiv3\pmod{16}\), and \(19\) itself is less than each of \(32,64,128\). Therefore
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19
      =10+57
      =67.
\]

Next compute \(F(2055)\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Also
\[
2055=2048+7.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(1\le k\le11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2048=2^{11}\). Hence \(2055\bmod 2^k=7\bmod 2^k\). For \(k=1\) this residue is \(1\), for \(k=2\) it is \(3\), and for every \(k=3,4,\ldots,11\) it is \(7\), because \(7<2^k\). There are nine integers from \(3\) through \(11\), inclusive. Consequently
\[
F(2055)=1+3+\underbrace{7+7+\cdots+7}_{9\text{ terms}}
       =1+3+9\cdot7
       =4+63
       =67.
\]

The indices are distinct, since \(147\ne2055\). They also both lie in the counting range for \(a(67)\): plainly \(147<2055<4096=2^{12}<2^{68}\). Thus the set
\[
\{m:0\le m<2^{68}\text{ and }F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\). Its cardinality is therefore at least \(2\), and hence
\[
a(67)\ge2.
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) is one of the numbers in
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts in particular that \(a(67)=1\), whereas the two explicit occurrences above show that \(a(67)\ge2\). This contradiction disproves the conjecture.
